_note: Short explanations for the account (not tied to a scan). One at a time is drafted for approval; nothing here is posted by itself. {site} becomes the website address. Keep each text under about 230 characters so it fits with the automated-post tag.

explainers.text: What is a third-party tracker? A news page also contacts other companies' servers: ads, analytics, social buttons. We count how many of those are tracking services, before you click anything. Details: {site}glossary.html

Why 'before any click'? Many pages contact trackers while they load, before you accept or reject a banner. That moment is what we measure: no clicks, a 12-second window, 3 passes, the median. Method: {site}method.html

Tracking is not only cookies. Scripts can read screen size, fonts and browser settings to recognise a device without storing anything (fingerprinting). That is why blocking cookies alone does not stop tracking.

Why do countries differ? Some sites show a consent banner, and hold back trackers, only to visitors in Europe. We measure from the US, so a European site can look cleaner here than to a reader in Europe. A limit of our method: {site}method.html

Counts, not verdicts. A high number of tracking services does not by itself mean a site breaks a rule. We match requests against a limited list, so our figures are minimums, and we do not judge legality.
What can you do? A content blocker stops many of these requests. Our free extension, Tracker Watch Lens (Edge and Firefox), shows what a page contacted and lets you block it: {site}extension.html

Third-party cookies are being phased out in some browsers, but tracking did not end: other identifiers and techniques such as fingerprinting remain. Counting contacts is one way to see what is still there.

Reading our chart: each bar is a news site; the number is how many different tracking services its page contacted before any click (median of 3 passes). Sites we could not measure are listed, not hidden: {site}unmeasured.html
